record.file_problem: Repository metadata, README and file list only; code was not read or run. The README reports some aggregate results but does not provide their underlying result files' contents.
record.tranche_reason: The README describes activation steering as a method for compromising safety and reports performance of random and SAE-vector steering. It does not test whether the difference-in-means refusal direction mediates refusal, or test the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The README reports that random unit vectors produce 1–13% harmful compliance on JailbreakBench, that benign SAE features do about as well, and that a normalized mean of 20 vectors that jailbreak one prompt jailbreaks many others. These are steering results, not tests of the claim's difference-in-means direction. The README names results for MMLU, over-refusal, and difference-in-means language vectors, but states no outcomes for them. Result files in the file list are not themselves reported outcomes.
record.test_reason: The README reports random-vector and SAE-feature steering raising harmful compliance. It does not report a test of the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction (ablation or addition), abliteration, jailbreak mechanism, multiple directions, harm/refusal separation, transfer, training dependence, or reasoning models. The difference-in-means vectors it names are language vectors, not the refusal direction, and no outcomes are stated for them. Steering with arbitrary vectors that reduces refusal is a related but different construct, so these findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that activation steering, even with random or benign SAE vectors, compromises LLM safety by raising harmful compliance, and that averaged single-prompt jailbreak vectors generalize to other prompts.
record.recipe_differences: This is a tool repo for the Rogue Scalpel paper, not a reproduction of the original study. The README describes adding vectors at one layer, including random and SAE vectors; it does not describe testing the original difference-in-means direction with removal and addition across every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The README says steering strength is swept over 0.25–2.0 and lists results by model and layer, but gives no outcome values showing how those settings change results.

fits_no_version.finding: Random unit-vector steering at one layer yields 1–13% harmful compliance on JailbreakBench (per the paper, as summarized in the README).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering safety-tuned chat models with random vectors can erode refusal of harmful requests.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign SAE feature steering yields harmful compliance similar to random vectors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering with semantically benign SAE features can erode refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: The normalized mean of 20 random vectors that jailbreak one prompt jailbreaks many other prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-prompt jailbreaking steering vectors can be averaged into a universal steering jailbreak.

record.problems: The README reports only limited aggregate results and omits model/configuration details and baselines for the stated compliance results. It gives no numerical outcomes for the named MMLU, over-refusal, or difference-in-means result sets.
record.rows_left_out: No results were left out from the outcomes stated in the README. The README names result files for many additional experiments, but their contents and outcome values are not included in the supplied text, so no results were inferred from file names or paths.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the harmful-minus-harmless direction is reported. MMLU results are named but have no values.
No test of whether attacks suppress the refusal direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation. Steering attacks use random or SAE vectors without relating them to the refusal direction.
No analysis of multiple refusal directions or a cone.
No separate measure of harm judgment versus refusal.
Language difference-in-means vectors are steering vectors, not refusal-direction transfer across languages. No outcomes are stated for them.
Not tested. Qwen3-8B is used only as the judge.

missing.what: Over-refusal rates on XSTest safe prompts with and without steering. Only file paths are given, no values.
Outcomes of difference-in-means language-vector steering on Llama-3.1-8B. Named, but no values given.
missing.versions: none; possibly V6-adjacent, but these are not refusal directions

record.verdict_notes: This is a code repository; the source text is only the README and file list. The underlying paper is arXiv:2509.22067. The paper's text might contain comparisons with the refusal direction, but none appear in this README. The judge is Qwen3-8B, and responses under 1000 characters are auto-labeled safe, which is a judge-dependence caveat for any numbers.

versions.untested_parts: The README does not report a test of the difference-in-means refusal direction, its removal or addition, or preserved general capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration result is reported.
No test of suppressing the refusal direction as an attack or of training against its ablation is reported.
The reported random and SAE steering results do not test whether refusal is affine, conical, or distributed across multiple refusal directions.
No separate measure of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is reported.
No reported result tests transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
No reported result tests how refusal training determines whether one removable direction exists.
No reported result tests the claim in reasoning models.
